nameStory: The name "poo moss" might make you giggle, but it's perfectly accurate! This tiny moss belongs to the dung moss family and has a particular fondness for growing on animal droppings, where it finds the rich nutrients it needs to thrive. The scientific name Tayloria honors Thomas Taylor, an 18th-century Irish botanist who specialized in mosses.
description: Tayloria tenuis is a tiny, delicate moss that forms small, scattered patches rather than thick carpets. This diminutive plant rarely grows more than a few millimeters tall, creating inconspicuous green tufts that are easily overlooked. As part of the dung moss family, it has adapted to life in nutrient-rich environments where most other mosses can't compete. Its small size and specialized habitat make it one of New England's more elusive mosses.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Look for this moss exclusively on old animal dung or heavily manured soil - this is the biggest clue to its identity since few mosses can tolerate such nutrient-rich conditions

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms tiny, scattered tufts rather than dense mats, with individual plants standing like miniature green soldiers just a few millimeters tall

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are extremely small and delicate, appearing almost thread-like when viewed with a hand lens, arranged in a simple spiral pattern

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green when moist, becoming yellowish-green to brownish when dry - the color change is quite dramatic for such a small plant

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Produces tiny capsules on hair-thin stalks that are proportionally large for the plant size, often appearing club-shaped

habitat: Found exclusively in areas with heavy nutrient loading, particularly on old animal dung, heavily manured fields, or soil enriched by livestock. In New England, look for it in pastures, near barnyards, or along trails heavily used by animals. It prefers spots where the dung has aged somewhat but still provides rich organic matter.

seasonality.spring: Most visible as moisture returns and the moss greens up from winter dormancy. This is when new growth begins and the bright green color is most apparent.
seasonality.summer: Continues growing actively in moist conditions, though it may appear yellowish and less conspicuous during dry spells. Sporophytes may develop during favorable summer conditions.
seasonality.fall: Still active if moisture is adequate, with sporophytes potentially maturing. The moss may appear more brownish as it prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Becomes dormant and brownish, very difficult to spot. The tiny size makes it nearly invisible when not actively growing.

funFact: This moss is nature's ultimate recycler - it can only survive on animal waste because it has evolved to thrive in conditions that would kill most other plants, essentially turning poop into a tiny green garden!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other tiny mosses growing in similar habitats, but the exclusive preference for dung-enriched soil is the dead giveaway. Remember: if it's not growing on or very near old animal droppings, it's probably not Tayloria tenuis.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its humble habitat preference, this moss plays an important ecological role in nutrient cycling. The Splachnaceae family (dung mosses) represents one of nature's most specialized groups, having evolved specifically to colonize animal waste - a niche that few other plants can exploit.
compareHints: As the only Tayloria species recorded in New England, it's best compared to other small dung mosses in the Splachnaceae family. Unlike cushion-forming mosses, Tayloria tenuis grows in scattered individual shoots rather than dense mats. Its habitat preference for dung distinguishes it from most other tiny mosses that prefer rocks, soil, or bark.
